title: The Founding of Medecins Sans Frontieres
text:
Between 1968 and 1970 a group of young French doctors volunteered with the French Red Cross in Biafra, the region whose attempt to secede from Nigeria led to war and mass starvation. They were shocked by what they saw, and frustrated that the Red Cross, bound by its rule of neutrality and discretion, would not speak publicly about it. Some of them, among them Bernard Kouchner, began to speak out on their own.

Around the same time, after a devastating cyclone struck East Pakistan in 1970, the French medical journal Tonus, edited by Raymond Borel and Philippe Bernier, called for doctors to form a group that could respond quickly to disasters. The two groups came together.

On 22 December 1971 they founded Medecins Sans Frontieres, Doctors Without Borders, in Paris. Its founders committed it to providing medical care wherever it was needed, regardless of race, religion or politics, independently of governments, and, unlike the Red Cross, to speaking out about what its members witnessed.

The early years were chaotic and full of arguments about how far to go in speaking out, and about how professional the organization should become. In 1979 a bitter dispute led Kouchner and some others to leave and found a separate group. But the organization grew into one of the world's largest independent medical aid groups, working in war zones and epidemics in dozens of countries. In 1999 MSF received the Nobel Peace Prize.
lesson: Professionals who unite around clear principles can act where governments will not. Even a team torn by disagreement can grow if its core purpose stays clear.
people: Bernard Kouchner, Raymond Borel, Philippe Bernier and other founding doctors and journalists
source: MSF official histories; Renee C. Fox, Doctors Without Borders: Humanitarian Quests, Impossible Dreams (2014)
